The alcohol on the adjacent ring carbon can form a favorable six-membered O-H...O=C contact. Conformers 26, 15, and 5 have the best examples: H...O distances are about 1.87-1.91 A with D-H...A angles near 157 degrees. Conformers 13 and 28 retain strong contacts but with approximately 1.95 A distances and 149-150 degree angles, while 21 is somewhat weaker at about 2.03 A and 141 degrees; its carbonyl is also more tightly folded toward the ring. A second family uses the alcohol attached to the side-chain-bearing ring carbon to make a geometrically less favorable five-membered contact. Conformer 1 is best in this family at about 1.97 A and 138 degrees, followed by 29, 3, and 11 at roughly 2.05-2.07 A and 130-132 degrees, and 6 at about 2.14 A and 127 degrees. Conformers 12 and 22 have weaker carbonyl hydrogen bonds around 2.32-2.34 A and 125-126 degrees. Conformer 24 has a longer but similarly directed contact near 2.50 A; conformer 8 has two poorly aligned approaches to the carbonyl (approximately 2.48 and 2.63 A, with angles only about 117-121 degrees), providing some stabilization but requiring a compact fold. Conformers 17 and 4 have only marginal contacts near 2.8 A. In the remaining structures, the carbonyl and alcohol donors are too far apart or incorrectly oriented. Among these, 7, 19, 2, 10, 30, and 9 keep the carbonyl relatively extended from the ring and avoid close O...O repulsion, so they are preferred over the more compact non-hydrogen-bonded forms. Conformers 14, 25, 16, 27, and 23 are gauche/compact but lack a compensating donor alignment. Conformer 18 brings the carbonyl oxygen toward an alcohol oxygen without aiming its O-H bond at the acceptor, and 20 is least favorable because its approximately 2.96 A O...O approach has a badly bent O-H...O geometry near 112 degrees, giving crowding/dipole repulsion rather than an effective hydrogen bond. The ordering within the 26/15/5 group, within the 29/3/11 group, and especially among the non-hydrogen-bonded extended conformers is uncertain because their remaining differences are mainly small alcohol and methyl torsional effects.

The five-membered pyrrolic framework is essentially planar and has normal bond lengths in every structure, so there is no major ring-strain discriminator. Stability is therefore controlled mainly by rotation of the ethyl and hydroxymethyl substituents. First, the most favorable hydroxymethyl geometries keep O clear of both ring atoms flanking the substituent: conformer 21 is especially open, with O about 3.5–3.7 Å from the neighboring ring heavy atoms. Conformers 25, 17, 10, 23, 8, 16, 30, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 18 also have comparatively noncrowded O positions, generally with nearest relevant heavy-atom separations around 3.25–3.5 Å. Second, conformers 6, 15, 7, 12, 1, and 11 have somewhat less favorable contacts or torsions; 11 places O only about 3.05 Å from N, while 12 also has methyl-H/N-H approaches near 2.4 Å. Third, conformers 20, 22, 19, 26, 9, 28, 13, and 14 point O toward the carbon side of the ring, giving O···C distances near 2.97–3.0 Å and O···ring-H distances near 2.85 Å; these are mild steric/eclipsing penalties rather than catastrophic clashes. The closest N/O arrangements occur in 24, 27, and 29. Although 24 and 27 have H(N)···O distances near 2.40 Å, the N-H···O direction is roughly perpendicular rather than linear, so this is at best a weak, highly constrained interaction and does not fully compensate for N···O distances near 2.74–2.75 Å. Conformer 29 has a similarly short N···O distance, about 2.80 Å, but H(N)···O is around 3.0 Å, providing still less hydrogen-bond compensation. Ethyl rotamers with the terminal methyl directed toward a ring C-H were ranked slightly below the more open/N-side rotamers. Most adjacent entries are likely separated by small torsional-energy differences, so the central part of the ranking is substantially more uncertain than the broad open-versus-close-contact tiers.

Conformers 5 and 2 also keep these branches well separated, while 29 is very open and keeps the two oxygen atoms about 4.6 Å apart. The lowest group, 24, 4, 22, 8, and 12, folds the carbonyl-carbon and proximal alkyne-carbon regions to roughly 2.7–2.8 Å; 12 also has a relatively compact carbonyl–methyl arrangement. All geometries appear to be genuine staggered minima rather than grossly clashing structures, so ordering within the non-hydrogen-bonded middle and lower groups is substantially more uncertain than separation of the hydrogen-bonded top group.

The covalent geometries are all chemically reasonable, with no grossly distorted bonds or catastrophic nonbonded overlaps, so the main discriminator is the hydroxyethyl/ether geometry followed by side-chain torsional strain and tetrahydrofuran puckering. These form the leading tier; 5 and 3 combine the strongest geometry with relatively open ring/substituent arrangements, 23 has excellent directionality but a slightly longer O···O separation, 12 is somewhat more crowded around the adjacent methyl and side chain, and the more bent contacts lower 17 and especially 14. Among structures lacking a full hydrogen bond, 8 and 30 have the most favorable extended, approximately anti/anti side-chain arrangements and keep the two oxygens well separated. Conformer 27 has a shorter O–H···O approach than the remaining structures (H···O about 2.58 Å), but its angle is only about 119°; this is treated as a weak stabilizing contact that partly compensates for its folded, gauche-rich chain. The next broad tier contains structures with one principal side-chain gauche relationship. Conformers 11, 22, 16, and 13 retain comparatively open ring-to-side-chain arrangements; 9, 18, 7, and 19 instead place the first side-chain segment gauche but leave the terminal alcohol more extended. Conformers 6, 1, 25, 10, 15, and 29 are similar one-gauche alternatives but have somewhat more compact methyl/ring-oxygen or side-chain contacts, so their exact ordering is especially uncertain. The final tier—20, 26, 21, 24, 2, 28, and 4—has two folded/gauche relationships without a properly directed hydrogen bond. Their ether-to-alcohol oxygen separations are generally around 3.6–3.8 Å, too long or incorrectly oriented for useful hydrogen bonding, while retaining the torsional cost of folding. Within this tier, 20, 26, and 21 have somewhat less congested ring puckers; 2 has a closer but poorly directed oxygen approach, and 28 and 4 combine compact ring geometry with no compensating attraction. Differences within each non-hydrogen-bonded tier are likely small and sensitive to the electronic-structure method and environment.

The molecule is an acyclic aldehyde with a CH3–CH(CHO)–CH2–O–CH=NH backbone, so the main differences are rotations about C(aldehyde)–C*, C*–CH2, and CH2–O. First, conformers 20, 30, 29, and 12 form a compact six-membered pseudoring in which the imine nitrogen approaches the aldehyde carbon at 2.10–2.13 Å and at an N···C=O angle of about 101°, close to a Bürgi–Dunitz donor–acceptor geometry. This provides favorable n(N)→π*(C=O) interaction and head-to-tail dipole alignment. The nitrogen lone-pair approach is most nearly collinear in 20, followed by 30; 29 and 12 have similarly short contacts but somewhat less favorable lone-pair orientation and slightly tighter N···O crowding near 2.64 Å. Conformer 25 is the best nonfolded structure: both the carbonyl/ether-bearing backbone and the CH2–O–CH=N segment are close to anti, with the heteroatoms well separated and no important clash. Conformers 1, 3, and 13 also have an anti CH2–O torsion and extended geometries, though the ether oxygen is gauche to the carbonyl-bearing branch; 13 has the closer O···O arrangement and is placed slightly lower. Conformers 27, 5, 7, 23, and 22 keep the ether oxygen approximately anti to the carbonyl branch across C*–CH2, avoiding the worst heavy-group gauche interaction, but have a gauche or skew CH2–O–CH=N torsion. Conformers 16, 15, 8, and 11 have the favorable anti terminal ether torsion but place the ether oxygen anti to the central hydrogen, leaving it gauche to both carbonyl and methyl groups; 16 and 15 have less close carbonyl/ether oxygen dispositions than 8 and 11. Conformers 2, 18, and 6 show weaker, longer N···C=O approaches of roughly 2.8–3.0 Å at suitable carbonyl attack angles, partly compensating their gauche torsions. Conformers 24, 9, 4, 17, 28, and 21 lack a strong donor–acceptor contact and are ordered mainly by how extended their heavy-atom skeletons are; 21 is lowered by a relatively close carbonyl-O/ether-O arrangement. Conformers 26, 19, 10, and 14 put the ether oxygen anti to the small central hydrogen while also retaining a non-anti terminal ether torsion, producing two uncompensated heavy-group gauche relationships; 10 and 14 additionally have the closer O···O dispositions. No conformer has a convincing N–H···O hydrogen bond: the potentially short H···O cases have poor donor angles, while most are much too distant. The middle of the ranking is uncertain because the gauche penalties and dipole interactions are likely within a few tenths of a kcal/mol, and the placement of the four compact conformers depends especially on the strength assigned to the short n(N)→π*(C=O) contact.

The six-membered carbon ring is the dominant energetic feature. I first separated geometries with a regular staggered chair from distorted twist/boat-like rings by comparing the three transannular ring-carbon separations and the alternating puckering pattern. Conformers 3, 8, 15, 16, 19, 21, 24, 25, and 29 have the cleanest chair geometry and place both carbon substituents outward: the substituent carbons remain roughly 3.8-3.9 angstrom from the relevant 1,3 ring carbons, avoiding axial 1,3-diaxial contacts. These form the lowest tier. Within that tier, 8 and 21 have especially exposed C-O/O-H groups; 16, 29, and 15 are similarly uncluttered. In 24 and 3 the oxygen is slightly closer to a neighboring ring sector, while 25 has an O-H orientation somewhat more directed toward the ring. Conformer 19 has the closest oxygen approach to a nonbonded ring carbon in this tier, so it is placed last among these otherwise near-degenerate chairs. Conformers 5, 6, 9, 12, 13, 22, 26, and 27 also retain essentially ideal chair rings, but the hydroxymethyl carbon lies only about 3.1-3.3 angstrom from both flanking 1,3 ring carbons, identifying an axial or strongly pseudoaxial side chain. They therefore incur substantial 1,3-diaxial strain despite keeping the methyl group outward. Among them, 12, 26, and 13 have relatively exposed oxygen orientations; 9, 6, and 5 are intermediate; 27 folds the alcohol somewhat more toward the ring, and 22 has the closest oxygen-ring approach and an inward-directed O-H orientation. The remaining structures have twist-chair, twist-boat, or boat-like puckering, indicated by loss of the characteristic approximately 3.0 angstrom chair diagonal and less regular staggering. Their ring torsional strain should outweigh the small alcohol-rotamer differences. Conformer 7 is the best of this group because both substituents are comparatively pseudo-equatorial. Conformer 11 also reduces side-chain axial crowding. Conformers 23 and 4 have relatively exposed alcohol groups, whereas 1 has a more axial hydroxymethyl environment despite a somewhat less severe ring distortion. Conformers 17, 30, and 28 retain additional side-chain/ring proximity; 18 is more folded. Conformer 14 exchanges this for a strongly pseudoaxial methyl group, which is unfavorable. Conformers 2, 10, and especially 20 combine distorted ring puckering with inward-facing alcohol orientations and short O-H/ring-H or oxygen/ring approaches. There is no conventional intramolecular hydrogen bond because the alcohol is the only heteroatom; weak C-H...O contacts cannot be assigned enough weight to overcome chair and axial-equatorial effects. Ordering within each alcohol-rotamer subgroup is consequently uncertain, particularly among the first nine and among the final twist/boat structures.

1. All structures have normal covalent geometry and no true ring, so the main differences are backbone gauche/anti torsions, steric crowding around the branched carbon, and intramolecular hydrogen bonding. 2. The strongest stabilization is an alcohol O-H...O=C(formamide) contact. Conformers 30, 7, 21, and 8 have especially favorable contacts: H...O distances are about 1.87-1.92 Å with O-H...O angles near 162-170 degrees. Conformer 30 combines a nearly linear contact with relatively favorable extended backbone and methyl orientations; 7 has the shortest contact but a somewhat more folded chain; 21 and 8 are similarly competitive. 3. Conformers 23, 4, 9, and 14 also form O-H...O=C contacts. The contact in 23 is short but more bent; those in 4 and 9 are very linear but slightly longer, with 4 having the less crowded branched-carbon arrangement; 14 is both somewhat bent and associated with an additional gauche backbone arrangement. 4. Conformers 5 and 1 retain weaker O-H...O=C contacts near 2.1 Å and roughly 145-147 degrees. Conformer 5 has the better placement of the methyl substituent, whereas 1 is more compact and has several simultaneous gauche relationships. 5. Conformers 24, 6, 15, and 25 instead form N-H...O(alcohol) contacts. These are six-membered-chain closures with H...O distances around 1.9-2.0 Å but angles only about 143-146 degrees. They should be less stabilizing than the good alcohol-to-carbonyl contacts because the alcohol oxygen is a weaker acceptor. Conformer 24 has the best combination of short contact and branch orientation; 6 is short but more crowded; 15 and 25 have longer contacts, with 25 lacking a favorable large-substituent anti arrangement. The relative placement of these four versus weakly hydrogen-bonded 5 and 1 is uncertain. 6. Conformer 29 is the best non-hydrogen-bonded candidate because its central C-C-C-N segment and methyl-bearing torsion are comparatively extended/anti, reducing gauche and steric penalties. 7. Among the remaining non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 17, 3, 16, 11, 27, 28, and 13 generally place the larger CH2OH substituent anti to the continuing chain and are therefore favored over more compact alternatives. Conformer 22 has a favorable downstream torsion and a very weak, bent N-H...O approach, but not a genuine strong hydrogen bond. 8. Conformers 2, 10, 26, and 12 have progressively less favorable combinations of gauche torsions or compact branch placement. Conformers 18 and 19 place the smaller methyl group rather than CH2OH in the more favorable anti sector while retaining compact backbone arrangements. Conformer 20 is the most consistently folded non-hydrogen-bonded geometry, with no compensating donor-acceptor contact. 9. The first several hydrogen-bonded structures are close in estimated energy, and the ordering within the non-hydrogen-bonded group is particularly uncertain because it depends on sub-kcal/mol torsional, dispersion, and dipole effects that cannot be quantified reliably from coordinates alone.

1. The aziridine ring has nearly the same bond lengths and geometry throughout, so differential ring strain is small. The main discriminants are intramolecular hydrogen bonding, torsions about the C5-C12 and C12-C13 bonds, and short O/N nonbonded contacts.
2. Conformer 20 has the best overall balance: a strong six-membered O-H...O contact (H...O about 1.98 Å, angle about 139°), an anti relationship between the CH2OH and aziridine substituents, and good O/N separation. Conformer 18 has the only clear O-H...N interaction (H...N about 2.13 Å, angle about 151°); this is strong but is offset by a less favorable backbone torsion and a very short secondary O...N contact. Conformers 16, 12, 1, and 7 also combine good backbone staggering with strong O-H...O contacts. In 12 the hydrogen bond is especially short and linear (about 1.93 Å and 144°), but O...N is only about 2.77 Å.
3. Conformers 6, 21, 2, 13, 22, and 30 retain useful O-H...O hydrogen bonds but have either a less favorable large-group gauche relationship or a relatively close, non-hydrogen-bonded O...N approach. Conformer 6 has an excellent O-H...O geometry and well-separated O/N atoms, whereas 21 and 13 gain strong central-OH-to-primary-O contacts but use a less favorable backbone rotamer.
4. Conformers 11, 14, 10, 24, 9, 29, 27, and 4 form progressively weaker or more strained O-H...O contacts. Conformer 10 has a short hydrogen bond but also an unusually close O...N distance near 2.63 Å without proper proton alignment. The contacts in 29, 27, and 4 are longer or more bent, and their large substituents are not anti.
5. Conformer 15 has only a weak, bent OH...O approach (H...O about 2.40 Å, angle about 122°), but otherwise favorable torsions. Conformers 8 and 5 lack convincing hydrogen bonds, although their large substituents are comparatively well staggered. Conformers 25 and 17 have intermediate backbone arrangements but no compensating polar contact.
6. Conformers 3, 23, 19, 26, and especially 28 lack useful donor-acceptor alignment while retaining less favorable gauche arrangements. Conformer 28 also has an approximately 2.60 Å O...N contact with both heteroatom proton directions pointing away, making it the most likely to suffer lone-pair/steric repulsion.
7. The middle of the ranking is uncertain because many O-H...O contacts differ by only about 0.1 Å and 5-10 degrees, so labels 6/21/2/13 and 11/14/10/24 could interchange after electronic-structure optimization. Solvent could also weaken the advantage of the compact hydrogen-bonded conformers.

1. The molecule is acyclic, so the main differences are torsional strain and intramolecular hydrogen bonding rather than ring strain. The relevant flexible segment is O–C–C–C–C–OH. Anti torsions are generally preferred; multiple gauche torsions are penalized unless they create a favorable contact. 2. Conformers 3, 18, 20, 2, 12, and 13 fold the terminal OH back toward the imidate/ether oxygen. Their approximate H···O distances and O–H···O angles are respectively 1.87 Å/159°, 1.90 Å/154°, 1.91 Å/153°, 2.02 Å/154°, 2.09 Å/138°, and 2.22 Å/138°. Thus 3 has the best hydrogen-bond geometry, 18 and 20 are nearly tied, 2 is slightly weaker, and 12 and especially 13 have more bent, weaker contacts. These folded structures require three gauche-like backbone torsions, but the hydrogen bond should more than compensate for that in 3, 18, 20, and 2. 3. Conformer 23 has an essentially all-anti O–C–C–C–C–O backbone and no important close contact, making it the lowest-strain extended conformer. Its placement relative to weakly hydrogen-bonded 12 and 13 is uncertain and will depend strongly on dielectric environment. 4. Conformers 10 and 16 have two anti torsions and only a terminal-side gauche torsion; 8 and 17 likewise have two anti torsions but place the gauche bend nearer the imidate end. These four are low-strain and probably close in energy, with 10/16 given a slight steric advantage. 5. Conformers 28, 24, and 15 have a gauche–anti–gauche pattern with well-separated bends and relatively extended oxygen termini. Conformers 19 and 27 contain adjacent but helical rather than strongly syn-pentane-like gauche bends. Conformers 29, 25, and 11 are similar two-gauche structures but bring the two oxygenated ends somewhat closer, about 4.5 Å rather than about 5.2 Å, without forming a hydrogen bond; this gives a small electrostatic/steric penalty. 6. Conformer 14 has three gauche-like torsions but a weak N–H···O(terminal) contact, H···O about 2.45 Å with an angle near 128°. This is stabilizing but substantially poorer than the OH···O contacts above. 7. Conformers 22 and 26 are all-gauche but helical, avoiding the closest syn-pentane contacts. Conformers 7, 30, 9, and 4 have only two gauche torsions but one folded adjacent-gauche sequence, producing an approximately 3.0 Å nonbonded O···C contact; they are consequently close to 22/26 in estimated energy. 8. Conformers 21, 6, 5, and 1 combine three gauche torsions with tighter folding and no well-oriented strong hydrogen bond. Their internal O···O separations are only about 3.35–3.52 Å. Conformer 21 has a very weak, bent OH···O approach, so it is placed above 6 and 5; conformer 1 has the least productive dipole/H-bond orientation and is placed last. 9. The ordering within near-symmetry-related pairs and within the middle two-gauche group is intrinsically uncertain; the strongest distinctions are the good OH···O contacts at the top, the all-anti geometry of 23, and the unproductive compact all-gauche structures at the bottom.

The molecule is N≡C–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–cyclopropyl. All conformers retain similar cyclopropane bond lengths and angles, so the ring’s intrinsic strain is essentially constant; the ranking is governed mainly by the three backbone torsions C≡C–CH2–O–C, C–O–C–C, and O–C–C–cyclopropyl. There is no conventional hydrogen-bond donor. A gauche nitrile/ether torsion is tentatively favored by the alpha-alkoxy gauche/anomeric effect and occasional weak C–H···N contacts, while anti arrangements of the two longer alkyl-side torsions generally reduce steric and eclipsing interactions. Conformers 30 and 17 combine the favorable nitrile-side gauche orientation with anti, extended downstream torsions and have no important close contacts; they are nearly symmetry-related and form the leading pair. Conformers 6 and 15 retain an anti O–C–C–cyclopropyl segment and have an open, non-syn arrangement of the two ether-side gauche torsions, placing them next. The fully extended 2 and 27 avoid steric contacts but lose the proposed nitrile-side gauche stabilization. Conformers 26 and 5, followed closely by 16, 19, and 28, have gauche–anti–gauche backbones; 26/5 are the more extended variants, whereas the latter three fold the nitrile and cyclopropyl ends somewhat closer. Conformers 29, 12, and 9 are essentially equivalent anti–gauche–anti structures and remain relatively open. Among the all-gauche structures, 11, 1, 3, and 18 avoid the strongest syn-pentane-like approach and therefore precede more crowded variants. Conformer 23 has only one downstream gauche defect but lacks the nitrile-side gauche stabilization. Conformers 8 and 4 are geometrically open but contain two non-anti or appreciably displaced torsions. In 25, 24, and 10, opposite-sense adjacent gauche rotations bring the nitrile carbon and a downstream methylene to about 3.1 Å, producing a syn-pentane-like penalty, partly offset by weak C–H···N proximity. Conformers 20 and 13 require substantially displaced approximately 80–100 degree downstream torsions and also fold remote groups together. Conformers 7, 14, and 22 combine three gauche rotations with a short nitrile-carbon/downstream-carbon approach; 21 adds both this compact adjacent-gauche geometry and a strongly displaced terminal torsion, making it the least favorable estimate. Differences inside the near-symmetry-related groups are very uncertain, and the middle and lower groups could reorder because weak dispersion and C–H···N stabilization compete with small torsional penalties.

The connectivity is a hydroxymethyl-substituted, unsaturated seven-membered cyclic ether. Bond lengths and alkene geometry are reasonable in every structure, so the main discriminants are ring puckering/torsional strain and rotation of the CH2OH group. First, the ring geometries separate into four approximate strain classes using the repeated cross-ring 1,4 distances as proxies for staggered versus eclipsed torsions. Conformers 5, 16, 23, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29, and 30 have the most regular twist-chair-like rings: most diagnostic spans are about 2.99-3.19 Å, without a strongly compressed segment. Conformers 1, 3, 8, 9, 11, 13, 17, and 21 are slightly less regular, with spans extending to roughly 2.80 and 3.22 Å. Conformers 4, 6, 7, 15, and 19 are more asymmetric, including an approximately 3.29-3.30 Å span paired with an approximately 2.8 Å span. Conformers 2, 10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, and 26 are least favorable in ring geometry because one saturated segment is compressed to about 2.70-2.72 Å while another reaches about 3.24-3.25 Å, indicating the greatest eclipsing/torsional distortion. Second, within each ring class, CH2OH rotamers placing the hydroxyl oxygen anti to the more crowded saturated ring arm are mildly favored; this benefits 30, 27, 16, then 11, 21, 1, and later 10 and 26. Among outward rotamers, 24 and 5 have cleaner contacts than 25, 29, and 28. Conformer 23 has an H···O(ring) distance near 2.91 Å and an O-H···O angle near 129 degrees, providing a weak, bent intramolecular hydrogen bond that partly compensates for its less favorable side-chain rotamer. Conformer 7 has a similar weak contact and is preferred within its more distorted ring class. Conformer 28 instead brings the two oxygens to about 3.65 Å without useful hydrogen-bond directionality and also has a relatively close hydroxyl-O/ring-H contact, so it is placed last in the best ring class; conformer 6 has an analogous poorly directed oxygen approach. No structure has a short, nearly linear strong O-H···O hydrogen bond or an unmistakable catastrophic heavy-atom clash. Consequently, the ordering between adjacent structures within a ring class is uncertain and likely represents small energy differences; the broader ring-strain tiers are more reliable than the exact local ordering.

The common scaffold contains fused four-membered carbocyclic/oxetane rings, so all conformers retain appreciable intrinsic angle strain. Their ring bond lengths and butterfly puckering are broadly similar; no structure shows a uniquely catastrophic ring compression, making side-chain torsions and contacts the principal discriminants. Conformer 30 has the clearest intramolecular alcohol-to-ether hydrogen bond: H···O is about 2.00 Å, O···O about 2.94 Å, and O–H···O is nearly linear at about 169°. Conformer 15 has the same stabilizing motif but weaker geometry, with H···O about 2.05 Å and an angle near 154°, so it follows 30. Conformers 20 and 24 combine an extended O–C–C–ring arrangement with a favorable side-chain orientation away from the crowded fused-ring junction; 20 has the less crowded alcohol-H rotamer. Conformers 12, 14, and 10 are also extended and lack close nonbonded contacts, although their hydroxymethyl group lies nearer the more substituted bridgehead side; 12 has the most favorable O–H torsion of that set. The next tier consists primarily of staggered gauche O–C–C–ring conformers whose terminal oxygen points outward and avoids the ether oxygen and bridgehead region. Orientations represented by 1, 7, 6, 11, 3, and 23 place the carbon chain anti to the more crowded ring branch and are therefore preferred slightly over the analogous 19, 13, 8, 21, 9, and 27 set; 27 is penalized further because its alcohol oxygen approaches a ring carbon to roughly 3.2 Å without forming a hydrogen bond. Conformers 26, 29, 28, and 5 retain an anti terminal heavy-atom torsion but place the hydroxymethyl carbon gauche to both ring branches; 26 benefits from the least crowded O–H rotamer. The final group combines this more crowded exocyclic orientation with a gauche terminal torsion and no compensating hydrogen bond. Conformers 2, 25, and 16 have comparatively favorable O–H orientations, whereas 18, 17, 4, and 22 retain less favorable local contacts/torsions; 22 is placed last because the chain is folded toward the ring while its hydroxyl points away from the ether acceptor. Apart from the strongly hydrogen-bonded top pair and the most crowded bottom tier, differences are subtle and several neighboring entries could interchange after an electronic-structure energy calculation, especially because four-membered-ring puckering and alcohol torsional energies are small.

The cyclobutane rings have broadly similar modest butterfly puckering, so no conformer shows a uniquely severe ring-strain defect; the main discriminants are hydroxyl hydrogen bonding and side-chain torsions. Conformers 25, 19, 30, and 11 contain clear intramolecular O-H···O contacts: O···O distances are about 2.87-2.91 Å and H···O distances about 1.92-1.99 Å. The contacts in 25 and 19 are especially linear, while 30 is somewhat less tightly folded than 11 and also has the shorter contact, giving the order 25 > 19 > 30 > 11. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 21, 10, 22, 14, 18, and 9 have the most extended side chains and approximately anti O-C-C-C arrangements, minimizing gauche and ring-face crowding; 21 and 10 additionally have favorable primary-alcohol O-H rotamers. Conformers 4, 28, 17, and 13 retain an extended heavy-atom skeleton but have one gauche side-chain relationship; 4 and 28 keep the terminal oxygen relatively clear of the ring, whereas 13 places it closer to a ring carbon. Conformers 27, 6, 16, 7, 1, 26, 24, 3, 12, 29, and 2 are likewise extended but combine less favorable hydroxyl or side-chain rotamers; several of 26, 24, 3, 12, 29, and 2 bring the terminal oxygen nearer a ring carbon without gaining an O-H···O bond. Conformers 20, 8, 5, 23, and 15 fold the hydroxyethyl group toward the opposite side of the cyclobutane but fail to form a compensating hydrogen bond. This produces extra gauche/steric cost; 15 is the tightest such fold and has an unfavorable approximately 3.85 Å O···O approach. Differences within the extended non-hydrogen-bonded tiers are subtle and likely below roughly 1 kcal/mol, so their detailed order is substantially less certain than the hydrogen-bonded top tier and folded bottom tier.

1) All structures have the same O=CH–CH2–CH2–C≡C–aziridine framework. The aziridine C–C and C–N distances and pyramidal N geometry are nearly invariant, so differential ring strain is small. The N–H group remains too far from the aldehyde oxygen for a meaningful intramolecular hydrogen bond; thus the ranking is controlled mainly by the two saturated-chain torsions. 2) Conformers 13, 23, and 7 combine the favored coplanar/syn aldehyde arrangement [O···second-CH2 distance about 2.82 Å, consistent with a weak C–H···O contact rather than a hard clash] with an extended anti central torsion [carbonyl-C···first-alkyne-C about 3.79 Å]. They have the least torsional and steric strain and are essentially degenerate. 3) Conformers 22, 4, 15, 14, and 12 retain the extended central torsion but rotate the aldehyde-adjacent bond; O···second-CH2 is about 3.54–3.55 Å and O···alkyne-C about 4.77 Å. They are very open and clash-free, but lose the preferred aldehyde-side arrangement, placing them just below the first family. 4) Conformers 1 and 6 retain the favorable aldehyde-side geometry but use a gauche central torsion. This folds the first alkyne carbon toward oxygen (about 3.03 and 3.01 Å, respectively), so 1 is slightly preferred to 6. 5) The large family 29, 19, 16, 25, 30, 26, 10, 5, 20, 17, 8, 2, 21, 18, and 3 has both torsions gauche-like but with compatible signs: the carbonyl-C···alkyne-C separation remains near 3.0 Å while O···alkyne-C stays near 4.2 Å. These avoid a direct endpoint clash but pay two torsional penalties; differences inside this family are minute and the listed order mainly favors slightly larger 1,4 heavy-atom separations and less distorted torsions. 6) Conformers 11, 9, 27, and 24 are the more compact gauche/gauche combination, with O···alkyne-C only about 3.8 Å, and are therefore placed below the more open gauche/gauche structures. Conformer 28 is most strained: its carbonyl-C···alkyne-C distance contracts to about 2.88 Å and O···alkyne-C to about 3.55 Å, indicating the strongest pentane-like crowding and torsional distortion. Exact ordering within each near-degenerate family, especially the open gauche/gauche set, is uncertain without electronic energies.

1. The common scaffold is a strained oxetane ring bearing hydroxymethyl and –CH2–CHO substituents. Ring bond lengths and puckering are broadly similar across the set, with no unique ring distortion or severe atomic overlap, so the main differences arise from substituent torsions and intramolecular contacts. 2. Conformers 26, 7, and 2 have the clearest hydroxyl-to-carbonyl hydrogen bonds. Their H···O(carbonyl) distances and O–H···O angles are approximately 1.92 Å/163°, 2.04 Å/147°, and 1.94 Å/152°, respectively. Conformer 26 therefore has the best hydrogen-bond geometry. Conformer 7 is placed above 2 because its aldehyde orientation is more extended and less internally crowded, whereas 2 has a shorter bond but a less favorable folded/syn carbonyl torsion. 3. Conformers 24, 19, 11, 16, and 3 have shorter, constrained hydroxyl-to-ring-oxygen contacts: H···O distances are about 2.15–2.26 Å with angles near 109–113°. These are bent five-membered intramolecular contacts rather than strong linear hydrogen bonds, but they can stabilize the hydroxymethyl gauche geometry. Their aldehyde groups are also relatively extended, with ring-carbon···O(carbonyl) 1,4 separations near 3.5–3.6 Å. Conformer 24 has the shortest such H···O contact, followed by 19; the distinctions among 11, 16, and 3 are small. 4. Conformers 15 and 5 retain comparable hydroxyl-to-ring contacts but place the aldehyde oxygen closer to the ring-substituted carbon, about 2.82 Å, indicating a less favorable syn/folded aldehyde torsion; they therefore follow the preceding group. 5. Conformers 10, 20, 28, 29, and 18 have more weakly interacting hydroxyl/ring-oxygen arrangements, with O···O near 3.0 Å and H···O around 2.6 Å, but generally extended aldehyde geometries and no serious acceptor–acceptor crowding. Conformers 12, 13, 30, and 23 lack useful hydrogen bonds but are similarly open and have well-separated oxygen atoms; they are competitive middle-ranked structures. 6. Conformers 1, 6, 17, 25, 22, 8, and 14 contain progressively less favorable combinations of folded side chains, syn aldehyde torsions, or absent hydrogen bonding. In 1 and 25 the carbonyl and ring oxygens approach to roughly 3.8 Å; in 6, 17, 8, and 14 the carbonyl oxygen is in the shorter 1,4 arrangement near 2.8 Å. Conformer 22 also has a modest hydroxyl-O/carbonyl-O approach near 3.1 Å without proper donor alignment. 7. The least favorable structures have close acceptor–acceptor contacts without a correctly directed O–H bond. Hydroxyl-O···carbonyl-O distances are approximately 2.94 Å in 9, 2.83 Å in 27, 2.91 Å in 4, and 2.92 Å in 21. Conformers 9 and 27 receive some compensation from the bent hydroxyl-to-ring interaction, whereas 4 and especially 21 do not; 21 additionally has the less favorable compact aldehyde torsion. 8. The first three and last few assignments are the most geometrically distinct. Much of the middle ordering is uncertain because it depends on the energetic balance between weak, bent O–H···O contacts, gauche effects, aldehyde torsional preferences, and small dipole differences that cannot be quantified reliably from coordinates alone.

The epoxide bond lengths and three-membered-ring geometry are essentially invariant, so differential ring strain is not a major discriminator. The strongest feature is an intramolecular hydroxyl-to-amide-carbonyl hydrogen bond. Conformers 10 and 1 have H···O(carbonyl) distances near 1.87 Å and O-H···O angles of about 150–153 degrees; 10 is favored because the bulky epoxide and amide-sidechain groups are more nearly anti, whereas 1 has a tighter gauche C(epoxide)···N arrangement. Conformers 6 and 9 retain the same interaction but with longer H···O distances near 2.26–2.29 Å and angles near 129–132 degrees; 6 has the shorter, better-aligned contact and less crowded epoxide orientation. The next group uses the epoxide oxygen as acceptor. Among conformers with an otherwise favorable anti backbone, 18, 26, and 12 have O-H···O(epoxide) contacts of approximately 2.00/121 degrees, 2.12/116 degrees, and 2.17/113 degrees, respectively. Conformers 8, 2, and 15 instead form N-H···O(epoxide) contacts; 8 is best aligned at about 2.20 Å and 127 degrees, followed by 2 and 15. Conformer 24 has a short hydroxyl-to-epoxide contact near 2.11 Å but a more gauche backbone, placing it between 8 and 2. Conformers 28, 23, and 11 lack a compelling hydrogen bond but have relatively open, staggered geometries: their epoxide C and amide N are separated by roughly 3.8 Å, and the epoxide CH2 group is directed away from the sidechain. Conformers 4 and 25 gain weak, bent O-H···O(epoxide) contacts near 2.2 Å and 110 degrees, partially compensating for gauche crowding. Conformers 16, 7, 17, 19, and 3 retain an anti epoxide/amide relationship but place the sidechain closer to both atoms of the epoxide; 16 is least crowded within this set, while 3 has the tightest overall arrangement and less favorable acceptor-dipole proximity. Conformer 30 has only a weak, bent hydroxyl-to-epoxide contact near 2.32 Å and 107 degrees. Conformers 22 and 20 are open but gauche and lack a useful donor-acceptor alignment. Conformers 29 and 5 have additional sidechain/epoxide crowding; the very bent contact in 29 provides little stabilization. Conformers 14, 27, and 13 have especially short nonbonded C(epoxide)···N separations around 2.8–2.9 Å without a compensating hydrogen bond. Conformer 21 is placed last because its hydroxyl and epoxide oxygens are close, about 2.97 Å, while the O-H bond points away from the epoxide oxygen, leaving acceptor-acceptor/dipolar crowding together with a gauche backbone. The middle and lower portions are uncertain because most differences there are small torsional and electrostatic effects rather than distinct strong interactions.

The molecule is a cyclopropanol-substituted chain terminating in a second cyclopropane. All conformers retain comparable cyclopropane C-C distances and bond angles, so there is no clear outlier with substantially greater ring strain. There is also only one oxygen, present as an alcohol, so no conventional intramolecular hydrogen bond is possible; O-H orientation mainly changes weak steric and C-H/O contacts. The dominant discriminator is the dihedral along the four-carbon segment joining the substituted ring carbons.
